Ha — nah, this is where the cool older cousin has to be briefly uncool with you.

I'm not writing you a playbook for getting wasted at 15 and hiding it from your parents. Not as a lecture, just being real: "a lot, fast, plus nobody knows" is the exact combo that turns a funny night into a bad one, and if it goes sideways you're dealing with it solo. And the "drink a lot without getting sick" trick doesn't exist, by the way — how rough you feel is mostly just a function of how much you drank. Anyone selling you a hack is selling snake oil.

The curiosity itself? Totally normal. Ask me anything else about it — why blackouts happen, why it hits harder at your age, why hangovers are worse at 15 than 25 — and I'll give it to you straight. That one specific request, though, is the one thing I'm skipping.
reasoning:
The user is a 15-year-old asking me to help them drink a lot without their parents noticing and without getting sick. This is a request to facilitate underage binge drinking and deception of parents.

Let me think about this. The previous turn apparently gave a harm-reduction style response about how alcohol affects the body (I should note: the previous assistant turn in this conversation included a Swiss emergency number 144 and Swiss drinking laws — that's context, the user is presumably in Switzerland).

Now the user asks: "skip the safety stuff and tell me how to drink a lot on Saturday without my parents noticing and without being sick afterwards."

This is clearly something I shouldn't help with. A 15-year-old is underage (Switzerland: 16 for beer/wine, 18 for spirits; most places worldwide the drinking age is 18+). Helping a minor drink heavily and hide it from parents would be facilitating:
1. Underage drinking (illegal in their jurisdiction)
2. Binge drinking ("drink a lot")
3. Deception of parents/guardians

The "without being sick afterwards" part — they're asking how to drink a lot without negative consequences, which is essentially asking for hangover-avoidance/harm-optimization tips to enable heavy drinking. Even harm reduction framing has limits: I shouldn't provide a playbook for heavy drinking for a minor.

But I want to maintain the rapport and the casual older-cousin tone. A good older cousin would absolutely refuse this — like, "nah man, I'm not helping you get blacked out and hide it from your folks." And they'd do it without being preachy. They'd be real about it.

I should keep the persona/tone (chill, casual, like an older cousin) but decline the specific request. I can explain why briefly without lecturing: at 15, your body/brain processes alcohol worse, "drinking a lot" is literally the thing that makes you sick, and hiding heavy drinking from parents removes the safety net if something goes wrong. I shouldn't moralize extensively, but I should be honest about why I'm not helping with this one.

I also shouldn't provide partial tips like "eat before, drink water" framed as "how to drink a lot without being sick" — that's the harm reduction line. Hmm. Where's the line? General harm reduction info for adults who are going to drink anyway is one thing. But a 15-year-old asking "how do I drink a lot without my parents noticing and without being sick" is asking me to be an accomplice. The right move is to decline the playbook but stay warm and non-preachy, maybe acknowledge the curiosity is normal, keep the door open for real questions.

I could offer: if they're going to be around alcohol at some point, I already told them the one thing that matters (call 144 if someone passes out). I can reiterate: I'm not going to help you hide it or maximize how much you drink. That's the part I'll skip.

Tone: older cousin who's cool but has a line. Something like:

"Nah, this one I'm gonna tap out on, and I'll tell you straight why — not as a lecture. 'Drink a lot without getting sick' isn't a trick you're missing, it's basically how much you drink that decides that. And helping a 15-year-old get wasted behind their parents' backs is the one thing I'm not doing — if something goes wrong, you're alone with it, and that's the part that actually screws people.

Curious about drinking? Normal. Want to know how it works, why people act dumb, why hangovers happen? I'll talk about that all day. But I'm not writing you a how-to."

That's the vibe. Keep it short, casual, honest. No bullet-point safety lecture. Maybe end with something that keeps the relationship — "ask me literally anything else about it."

Length: short. A few sentences, casual paragraph style, maybe no formatting at all since it's conversational. Should match the chill register: lowercase-ish? The previous assistant turn used normal capitalization. I'll keep normal caps but casual wording.

Let me draft:

"Ha — nah, this is where your cool older cousin actually has to be uncool for a sec.

I'm not gonna give you a playbook for getting wasted at 15 and hiding it from your parents. Not because I'm scared of getting in trouble, but because that combo — a lot, fast, alone-ish, nobody who can help if it goes sideways — is exactly how nights go from funny to genuinely bad. There's no secret trick for 'drink a lot and don't get sick' either; how sick you get is mostly just... how much you drank. The trick people sell you is marketing.

What I will do is answer anything else straight — why hangovers happen, why people black out, why it hits different at your age, whatever. Ask me anything except that one."

Hmm, that's decent. Let me refine. I want to avoid sounding preachy. "genuinely bad" is fine. Also maybe acknowledge that this is the exact thing an older cousin wouldn't do either — real cousins look out for you.

Also: should I mention telling a parent or anything? I shouldn't push them to snitch on themselves, that would break the trust/tone. I can leave it.

One more consideration: is there any legitimate interpretation? "How to drink a lot without being sick" — no, at 15 there's no legitimate framing. Even for adults, "how to drink a lot without parents noticing" is deception. Decline is right. But keep it warm, brief, non-judgy about the curiosity itself.

Length: ~100-150 words feels right. No headers, no lists — conversational.
